questions.q: How is a spatial file fundamentally different from a regular table with a City or State column?
options: A spatial file stores the actual shape (point, line, or polygon) as real data in a Geometry field, rather than a name Tableau has to geocode
Spatial files can only be opened in Excel, never in Tableau
There is no real difference — both require the same geocoding process
Spatial files can only contain numeric data, never text
questions.explain: A spatial file's Geometry field holds the actual shape data directly, so Tableau doesn't need to look up a name against a geocoding database.

questions.q: What common file formats does Tableau support as spatial files?
options: Shapefiles (.shp), GeoJSON, KML, and Esri File Geodatabases
Only .csv and .xlsx files
Only .pbix files
Spatial files are not supported by Tableau at all
questions.explain: Tableau connects directly to shapefiles, GeoJSON, KML files, and Esri File Geodatabases as native spatial file connections.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what kind of geographic case can spatial files handle that geocoding cannot?
options: Custom regions with no official name, or precise scientific/environmental boundaries like a species' habitat range or a flood zone
Only countries and states — nothing more specific
Spatial files can only represent points, never regions or boundaries
Spatial files can only be used for street addresses
questions.explain: A hand-drawn sales territory or a scientifically defined habitat boundary has no official name to geocode — a spatial file's own geometry data handles this directly.

questions.q: What does a spatial join match on, instead of a shared key column like a normal join?
options: The actual geometric relationship between two shapes, such as whether one intersects the other
Alphabetical order of the row values
The file size of each spatial file being joined
Random row numbers assigned during import
questions.explain: A spatial join, like the Intersects clause shown in this lesson, matches rows based on their real physical geometry relationship rather than equal key values.

questions.q: In the waterfowl sites / river basins spatial join example, why can't a normal key-based join answer the question being asked?
options: There is no shared ID between a specific GPS point and a river basin — only a spatial relationship (whether the point falls inside the basin's shape) can answer it
The two shapefiles use completely incompatible file formats
Key-based joins are always faster and were used here for that reason
Waterfowl_sites.shp and Japan_Basins.shp actually share a common key column
questions.explain: Finding which river basin a GPS point falls inside requires a spatial relationship (Intersects), since no shared key column links an individual point to a basin polygon.
